questions.q: How does a Queueable job chain into a follow-up job?
options: Its execute method calls System.enqueueJob again, submitting a new Queueable instance as its last action
By annotating the class with @future(chain=true)
Chaining isn't possible with Queueable Apex — only Batch Apex supports it
By calling Database.executeBatch from inside execute
questions.explain: A Queueable job chains by calling System.enqueueJob again from inside its own execute method, submitting the next job in the sequence.

questions.q: What is the chain-depth rule for Developer Edition and Trial orgs?
options: Chains are completely disabled in Developer and Trial orgs
The default maximum stack depth is 5 (the original job plus four chained re-queues), though this default can be overridden
Developer orgs allow unlimited chain depth, unlike production orgs
Chain depth is capped at exactly 2 in every org type, no exceptions
questions.explain: Production orgs have no hard-enforced chain-depth limit, but Developer Edition and Trial orgs default to a maximum stack depth of 5 — the original job plus four chained re-queues — which Salesforce's docs note can be overridden for specific use cases.

questions.q: Why does chaining code typically check Test.isRunningTest() before calling System.enqueueJob again?
options: Because chaining a Queueable job inside an already-running test context produces an error, so the check skips the chain call during tests
Test.isRunningTest() is required syntax on every Queueable class regardless of chaining
It has nothing to do with chaining — it's only used to disable logging
Because System.enqueueJob doesn't exist in test context at all
questions.explain: Enqueuing a second asynchronous job from inside a job already running in a test's execution context throws an error. The standard workaround checks Test.isRunningTest() and skips the chain call during tests.

questions.q: What does the optional delay parameter on System.enqueueJob(queueable, delay) do?
options: It sets a minimum delay, from 0 to 10 minutes, before the chained job becomes eligible to run (ignored during tests)
It permanently pauses the job until manually resumed from Setup
It sets the batch chunk size for the next job in the chain
It determines how many times the job will retry on failure
questions.explain: The delay overload sets a minimum wait, 0 to 10 minutes, before the chained job becomes eligible to run — useful for throttling or waiting on an external system to settle. The delay is ignored when running inside a test.

questions.q: What is the real risk of a Queueable chain with no explicit stopping condition?
options: It can rapidly consume the org's shared daily limit on asynchronous Apex executions, which is shared across every future method, Queueable job, Batch Apex run, and Scheduled Apex execution
It will cause a compile-time error the moment the class is saved
It has no real risk, since chains automatically stop after exactly 5 links in every org
It only risks slowing down synchronous Apex, never asynchronous Apex
questions.explain: A chain with no stopping condition — or no throttling — can burn through the org's shared daily asynchronous Apex execution limit, which affects every other future method, Queueable job, Batch Apex run, and Scheduled Apex execution in the org for the rest of the day.
